entries.b8b0a2bae7429424e72b84ce9634998e0bcc4880: <div sID="gen8093" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="2Chr.10" sID="2Chr.10"/> <div eID="gen8093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8094" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8095" type="x-p"/> This chapter is copied almost verbatim from <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.19 2Chr.10.1-2Chr.10.19">1 Kings xii. 1-19</reference>, where it was opened at large. Solomon's defection from God was not repeated, but the defection of the ten tribes from his family is, in this chapter, where we find, I. How foolish Rehoboam was in his treating with them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.5-2Chr.10.14">5-14</reference>. II. How wicked the people were in complaining of Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.10.2-2Chr.10.4">ver. 2-4</reference>) and forsaking Rehoboam, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.16-2Chr.10.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. III. How just and righteous God was in all this, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.15">ver. 15</reference>. His counsel was thereby fulfilled. With him are strength and wisdom; both the deceived and the deceiver (the fool and the knave) are his (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job xii. 16</reference>), that is, are made use of by him to suit his purposes.
entries.4f48b6ec7d016dccef3fde506d1945de47928bc1: <div eID="gen8095" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8094" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Rehoboam Succeeds Solomon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 975.)</title> <div sID="gen8096" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Rehoboam went to Shechem: for to Shechem were all Israel come to make him king. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it came to pass, when Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Egypt, whither he had fled from the presence of Solomon the king, heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that Jeroboam returned out of Egypt. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they sent and called him. So Jeroboam and all Israel came and spake to Rehoboam, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he said unto them, Come again unto me after three days. And the people departed. <hi type="super">6</hi> And king Rehoboam took counsel with the old men that had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, What counsel give ye <hi type="italic">me</hi> to return answer to this people? <hi type="super">7</hi> And they spake unto him, saying, If thou be kind to this people, and please them, and speak good words to them, they will be thy servants for ever. <hi type="super">8</hi> But he forsook the counsel which the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men that were brought up with him, that stood before him. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto them, What advice give ye that we may return answer to this people, which have spoken to me, saying, Ease somewhat the yoke that thy father did put upon us? <hi type="super">10</hi> And the young men that were brought up with him spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou answer the people that spake unto thee, saying, Thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou <hi type="italic">it</hi> somewhat lighter for us; thus shalt thou say unto them, My little <hi type="italic">finger</hi> shall be thicker than my father's loins. <hi type="super">11</hi> For whereas my father put a heavy yoke upon you, I will put more to your yoke: my father chastised you with whips, but I <hi type="italic">will chastise you</hi> with scorpions. <div eID="gen8096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8097" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. The wisest and best cannot give every body content. Solomon enriched and advanced his kingdom, did all (one would think) that could be done to make then happy and easy; and yet either he was indiscreet in burdening them with the imposition of taxes and services, or at least there was some colour of reason to think him so. No man is perfectly wise. It is probable that it was when Solomon had declined from God and his duty that his wisdom failed him, and God left him to himself to act in this impolitic manner. Even Solomon's treasures were exhausted by his love of women; and probably it was to maintain them, and their pride, luxury, and idolatry, that he burdened his subjects. 2. Turbulent and ungrateful spirits will find fault with the government, and complain of grievances, when they have very little reason to do so. Had they not peace in Solomon's time? They were never plundered by invaders, as formerly, never put in fear by the alarms of war, nor obliged to hazard their lives in the high places of the field. Had they not plenty—meat enough, and money enough? What would they more? <hi type="italic">O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint!</hi>—<hi type="italic">O happy, if they knew their happy state!</hi> And yet they complain that Solomon made their yoke grievous. If any complain thus of the yoke of Christ, that they might have a pretence to break his bands in sunder and cast away his cords from them, we are sure that he never gave them any cause at all for the complaint, whatever Solomon did. <hi type="italic">His yoke is easy, and his burden is light.</hi> He never <hi type="italic">made us serve with an offering, nor wearied us with incense.</hi> 3. Many ruin themselves and their interests by trampling upon and provoking their inferiors. Rehoboam thought that because he was king he might assume as much authority as his father had done, might have what he would, and do what he would, and carry all before him. But, though he wore his father's crown, he wanted his father's brains, and ought to have considered that, being quite a different man from what his father was, he ought to take other measures. Such a wise man as Solomon may do as we will, but such a fool as Rehoboam must do as he can. The high-mettled horse may be kicked and spurred by him that has the art of managing him; but, if an unskilful horseman do it, it is at his peril. Rehoboam paid dearly for threatening, and talking big, and thinking to carry matters with a high hand. It was Job's wisdom, as well as his virtue, that he <hi type="italic">despised not the cause of his man-servant or maid-servant,</hi> when they argued with him (<reference osisRef="Job.31.13">Job xxxi. 13</reference>), but heard them patiently, considered their reasons, and gave them a soft answer. And a similar tender consideration of those in subjection, and a forwardness to make them easy, will be the comfort and praise of all in authority, in the church, in the state, and in families. 4. Moderate counsels are generally wisest and best. Gentleness will do what violence will not do. Most people love to be accosted mildly. Rehoboam's old experienced counsellors directed him to this method (<reference osisRef="2Chr.10.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be kind to this people, and please them, and speak good words to them,</hi> and thou art sure of them for ever." Good words cost nothing but a little self-denial, and yet they purchase good things. 5. God often fulfils the counsels of his own wisdom by infatuating men, and giving them up to the counsels of their own folly. No more needs to be done to ruin men than to leave them to themselves, and their own pride and passion.
entries.11c85d3422303dd5ab2b18d0481952d56c839603: <div eID="gen8097" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rehoboam's Folly. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 975.)</title> <div sID="gen8098" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king bade, saying, Come again to me on the third day. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the king answered them roughly; and king Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men, <hi type="super">14</hi> And answered them after the advice of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add thereto: my father chastised you with whips, but I <hi type="italic">will chastise you</hi> with scorpions. <hi type="super">15</hi> So the king hearkened not unto the people: for the cause was of God, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> might perform his word, which he spake by the hand of Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when all Israel <hi type="italic">saw</hi> that the king would not hearken unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David? and <hi type="italic">we have</hi> none inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to your tents, O Israel: <hi type="italic">and</hi> now, David, see to thine own house. So all Israel went to their tents. <hi type="super">17</hi> But <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the children of Israel that dwelt in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then king Rehoboam sent Hadoram that <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the tribute; and the children of Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. But king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to <hi type="italic">his</hi> chariot, to flee to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Israel rebelled against the house of David unto this day. <div eID="gen8098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8099" type="x-p"/> We may learn here, 1. That when public affairs are in a ferment violent proceedings do but make bad worse. Rough answers (such as Rehoboam here gave) do but stir up anger and bring oil to the flames. The pilot has need to steer steadily in a storm. Many have been driven to the mischief they did not intend by being too severely dealt with for what they did intend. 2. That, whatever the devices and designs of men are, God is, by all, doing his own work, and fulfilling the word which he has spoken, no iota or tittle of which shall fall to the ground. The cause of the king's obstinacy and thoughtlessness was <hi type="italic">of God, that he might perform the word which he spoke by Ahijah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.15">v. 15</reference>. This does not at all excuse Rehoboam's folly, nor lessen the guilt of his haughtiness and passion, that God was pleased to serve his own ends by them. 3. That worldly wealth, honour, and dominion, are very uncertain things. <hi type="italic">Solomon reigned over all Israel,</hi> and, one would think, had done enough to secure the monarchy entire to his family for many ages; and yet he is scarcely cold in his grave before ten of the twelve tribes finally revolt from his son. All the good services he had done for Israel were now forgotten: <hi type="italic">What portion have we in David?</hi> Thus is the government of Christ cast off by many, notwithstanding all he has done to bind the children of men for ever to himself; they say, <hi type="italic">We will not have this man to reign over us.</hi> But this rebellion will certainly be their ruin. 4. That God often visits the iniquities of the fathers upon the children. Solomon forsakes God, and therefore not he, but his son after him, is forsaken by the greatest part of his people. Thus God, by making the penal consequences of sin to last long and visibly to continue after the sinner's death, would give an indication of its malignity, and perhaps some intimation of the perpetuity of its punishment. He that sins against God not only wrongs his soul, but perhaps wrongs his seed more than he thinks of. 5. That, when God is fulfilling his threatenings, he will take care of that, at the same time, promises do not fall to the ground. When Solomon's iniquity is remembered, and for it his son loses ten tribes, David's piety is not forgotten, nor the promise made to him; but for the sake of that his grandson had two tribes preserved to him. The failings of the saints shall not frustrate any promise made to Christ their Head. They shall be chastised, but the covenant not broken, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.31-Ps.89.34">Ps. lxxxix. 31-34</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Chr.10"/> <div eID="gen8099" type="x-p"/>

entries.c45383bd85b2cf7179ef8cd50ad4adab720b773d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3979"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.1-2Chr.10.15">2Ch 10:1-15</reference>. Rehoboam Refusing the Old Men's Good Counsel.<div eID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3979"/><hi type="bold">1. Rehoboam went to Shechem--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1">1Ki 12:1</reference>). This chapter is, with a few verbal alterations, the same as in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.19">1Ki 12:1-19</reference>. <div eID="gen5746" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5242425f9d90714656adab748e7f1be354ae4c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3980"/><div sID="gen5747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3980"/><hi type="bold">3. And they sent--</hi>rather, "for they had sent," &c. This is stated as the reason of Jeroboam's return from Egypt. <div eID="gen5747" type="x-p"/>
entries.661dd3fab0485c68041156be58b70dd0e93f7f09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3981"/><div sID="gen5748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3981"/><hi type="bold">7. If thou be kind to this people, and please them, and speak good words to them--</hi>In the Book of Kings [1Ki 12:7], the words are, "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people, and wilt serve them." The meaning in both is the same, namely, If thou wilt make some reasonable concessions, redress their grievances, and restore their abridged liberties, thou wilt secure their strong and lasting attachment to thy person and government. <div eID="gen5748" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9003095315b795b7c208b0471048843d05155f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3982"/><div sID="gen5749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3982"/><hi type="bold">15-17. the king hearkened not unto the people, for the cause was of God--</hi>Rehoboam, in following an evil counsel, and the Hebrew people, in making a revolutionary movement, each acted as free agents, obeying their own will and passions. But God, who permitted the revolt of the northern tribes, intended it as a punishment of the house of David for Solomon's apostasy. That event demonstrates the immediate superintendence of His providence over the revolutions of kingdoms; and thus it affords an instance, similar to many other striking instances that are found in Scripture, of divine predictions, uttered long before, being accomplished by the operation of human passions, and in the natural course of events. <chapter eID="2Chr.10"/>

entries.ae7279c5514888001381d4c46ea224f856e9f0ab: <div eID="gen14109" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14110" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14110" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> The people apply to Rehoboam to ease them of their burdens, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.1-2Chr.10.4">2Chr 10:1-4</reference>. Rejecting the advice of the aged counsellors, and following that of the young men, he gives them an ungracious answer, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.5-2Chr.10.14">2Chr 10:5-14</reference>. The people are discouraged, and ten tribes revolt, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.15-2Chr.10.17">2Chr 10:15-17</reference>. They stone Hadoram, who went to collect the tribute; and Rehoboam but barely escapes, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.18">2Chr 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.19">2Chr 10:19</reference>. <div eID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> Rehoboam went to Shechem - This chapter is almost word for word the same as 1 Kings 12:1-19, to the notes on which the reader is referred.
entries.676d73b3f732227da8dbc89dc87bcf9fe2207634: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> My little finger shall be thicker - "My weakness shall be stronger than the might of my father." - Targum.
entries.4233390836fa5baa0217f4c3db5bfa47d87b767e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> For the cause was of God - "For there was an occasion Divinely given." - Targum.
entries.1f241c02c8b619c3793d88ddbca7b382c7ecf1d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14117" type="x-p"/> To your tents, O Israel - "To your cities, O Israel." - Targum. <div eID="gen14117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14118" type="x-p"/> Now, David, see to thine own house - "Now, David, rule over the men of thy own house." - Targum.
entries.693874be90ab359a2dbe39a0f560bd136bb60640: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14119" type="x-p"/> Stoned him - When he endeavored to collect the tribute which Solomon had imposed on them. - Jarchi.
entries.a8c3a7e63b84dc0b3faca69ab93ce084edb857b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen14119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14120" type="x-p"/> Israel rebelled - A few soft words, and the removal of a part of the oppressive taxes, (for they said, Ease thou Somewhat the grievous servitude), would have secured this people to the state, and prevented the shedding of a sea of human blood, which was the consequence of the separation of this kingdom. Rehoboam was a fool; and through his folly he lost his kingdom. He is not the only example on record: the Stuarts lost the realm of England much in the same way; and, by a different mode of treatment, the House of Brunswick continues to fill the British throne. May the thread of its fortune, woven by the hand of God, never be undone! and may the current of its power glide on to the latest posterity! <div eID="gen14120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14121" type="x-p"/> Talia secla, suis dixerunt, currite, fusis <div eID="gen14121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14122" type="x-p"/> Concordes stabili fatorum numine Parcae. <div eID="gen14122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14123" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. iv., ver. 46. "God's firm decree, by which this web was spun, <div eID="gen14123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14124" type="x-p"/> Shall ever bless the clue, and bid it smoothly run." <div eID="gen14124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14125" type="x-p"/> Labitur, et labetur in omne volubilis Aevum. <div eID="gen14125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14126" type="x-p"/> Horat. Epist., l. i., c. 2, v. 43. "Still glides the river, and shall ever glide." <div eID="gen14126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14127" type="x-p"/> Amen! Amen!  <chapter eID="2Chr.10"/> <div eID="gen14127" type="x-p"/>

entries.19e847e840a49b601b0da9fe1a8d6361702a253c: <div eID="gen5971" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">IV. The History of the Kingdom of Judah Until Its Fall - 2 Chronicles 10-36.</title> <div sID="gen5972" type="x-p"/> After giving an account of the revolt of the ten tribes of Israel from the divinely chosen royal house of David (2 Chron 10), the author of the Chronicle narrates the history of the kingdom of Judah - to which he confines himself, to the exclusion of the history of the kingdom of the ten tribes - at much greater length than the author of the books of Kings has done. This latter portrays the development of both kingdoms, but treats only very briefly of the history of the kingdom of Judah, especially under its first rulers, and characterizes the attitude of the kings and people of Judah to the kingdom of Israel and to the Lord only in the most general way. The author of the Chronicle, on the other hand, depicts the development of Judah under Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat much more thoroughly, by communicating a considerable number of events which are omitted in the book of Kings. As we have already proved, the purpose of the chronicler was to show, according to the varying attitude of the kings of the house of David to the Lord and to His law, how, on the one hand, God rewarded the fidelity of the kings and of the people to His covenant with prosperity and blessing, and furnished to the kingdom of Judah, in war with its enemies, power which secured the victory; and how, on the other, He took vengeance for every revolt of the kings and people, and for every fall into idolatry and superstition, by humiliations and awful judgments. And more especially from the times of the godless kings Ahaz and Manasseh does our author do this, pointing out how God suffered the people to fall ever deeper into feebleness, and dependence upon the heathen world powers, until finally, when the efforts of the pious kings Hezekiah and Josiah to bring back the people, sunk as they were in idolatry and moral corruption, to the God of their fathers and to His service failed to bring about any permanent repentance and reformation, He cast forth Judah also from His presence, and gave over Jerusalem and the temple to destruction by the Chaldeans, and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judah to be led away into exile to Babylon. <div eID="gen5972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5973" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.1-2Chr.10.19">2Ch 10:1-19</reference> <div eID="gen5973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5974" type="x-p"/> This event is narrated in our chapter, except in so far as a few unessential differences in form are concerned, exactly as we have it in 1 Kings 12:1-19; so that we may refer for the exposition of it to the commentary on 1 Kings 12, where we have both treated the contents of this chapter, and have also discussed the deeper and more latent causes of this event, so important in its consequences. Rehoboam’s Reign - 2 Chronicles 11-12 <div eID="gen5974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5975" type="x-p"/> When the ten tribes had renounced their allegiance to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, and had made Jeroboam their king (1Ki 12:20), Rehoboam wished to compel them by force of arms again to submit to him, and made for this purpose a levy of all the men capable of bearing arms in Judah and Benjamin. But the prophet Shemaiah commanded him, in the name of the Lord, to desist from making war upon the Israelites, they being brethren, and Rehoboam abandoned his purpose (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.1-2Chr.11.4">2Ch 11:1-4</reference>, cf. 1Ki 12:21-24), and began to establish his dominion over Judah and Benjamin. His kingdom, moreover, was increased in power by the immigration of the priests and Levites, whom Jeroboam had expelled from the priesthood, and also of many God-fearing Israelites out of the ten tribes, to Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.13-2Chr.11.17">2Ch 11:13-17</reference>). Rehoboam also set his family affairs in order, by nominating from among his many sons, whom his wives had borne to him, Abijah to be his successor on the throne, and making provision for the others in different parts of the country (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.18-2Chr.11.23">2Ch 11:18-23</reference>). But when he had established his royal authority, he forsook the law of Jahve, and was punished for it by the inroad of the Egyptian king Shishak, who marched through his land with a numerous host, took Jerusalem, and plundered the palace and the temple (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.1-2Chr.12.11">2Ch 12:1-11</reference>), but without wholly ruining Judah; and Rehoboam was king until his death, and his son succeeded him on the throne (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.12-2Chr.11.16">2Ch 11:12-16</reference>). <div eID="gen5975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5976" type="x-p"/> The order in which these events are narrated is not chronological; they are rather grouped together according to their similarities. As Rehoboam began even in the third year of his reign to forsake the law of God, and King Shishak made war upon Judah as early as in his fifth year, the building of the fortresses may have been begun in the first three or four years, but cannot have been ended then; still less can the sons of Rehoboam have been provided for in the time before Shishak’s inroad.  <chapter eID="2Chr.10"/> <div eID="gen5976" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And they spake unto him, saying, If thou be kind to this people, and please them, and speak good words to them, they will be thy servants for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 But he forsook the counsel which the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men that were brought up with him, that stood before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And he said unto them, What advice give ye, that we may return answer to this people, which have spoken to me, saying, Ease somewhat the yoke that thy father did put upon us?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And the young men that were brought up with him, spake unto him, saying, thus shalt thou answer the people that spake unto thee, saying, thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> somewhat lighter for us: thus shalt thou say unto them, My little <ns0:hi>finger</ns0:hi> shall be thicker than my fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers loins.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 For whereas my father <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> put a heavy yoke upon you, I will put more to your yoke: my fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther chastised you with whips, but I <ns0:hi>will chastise</ns0:hi> you with scorpions.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 So Jeroboam and all the people came to Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hoboam on the third day, as the king bade, saying, Come again to me on the third day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And the king answered them roughly, and king Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And answered them after the advice of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vy, but I will add thereto: my father chastised you with whips, but I <ns0:hi>will chastise</ns0:hi> you with scor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pions.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 So the king hearkened not unto the people, for the cause was of God, that the LORD might perform his word which he spake by the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Kin. 11<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> hand of Abijah the Shilonite, to Jeroboam the son of Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And when all Israel <ns0:hi>saw</ns0:hi> that the king would not hearken unto them, the people answered the
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:347" />
king, saying, What portion have we in David? and we have none inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to your tents, O Israel: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> now Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid, see to thine own house. So all Israel went to their tents.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 But <ns0:hi>as for</ns0:hi> the children of Israel that dwelt in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then king Rehoboam sent Hadoram that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> over the tribute, and the children of Israel stoned him with stones, that he died: but king Rehoboam <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> made speed to get him up to <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riot, to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>lee to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And Israel rebelled against the house of Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid unto this day.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
